The Story of Pushpadatta the Deceitful

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the bestower of infinite happiness and lord of the three worlds, and I write the story of Pushpadatta the deceitful, to destroy the sin of deceit.

In the ancient and famous city of Ajitavart, King Pushpachul had a queen named Pushpadatta. Enjoying royal pleasures, Pushpachul one day heard the nature of Jain dharma from the monk Amarguru — the dharma that leads to the happiness of heaven and liberation. Hearing this discourse, Pushpachul became deeply detached from the world, the body, and sensual pleasures. He took initiation and became a monk. His queen Pushpadatta, following his example, also took the vows of an Aryika from the nun Brahmmila.

Yet even after taking vows, Pushpadatta retained her pride in her royal status. She began to act contrary to religious conduct. She considered bowing to other nuns as an insult to herself, so she refused to pay respects to anyone. Moreover, she adorned her body with various fragrant substances, despite being in a state where such adornment was inappropriate.

Seeing her unrighteous conduct, the virtuous Brahmmila one day advised her, "In your present state, adorning the body is not proper. These actions are against dharma and cause sin, for they increase desire for sensual objects." Pushpadatta replied, "No, I do not adorn myself. My body is naturally fragrant from birth." Truly, those whose hearts have no natural inclination toward dharma cannot be reformed by any amount of advice. Their tendencies only move toward worse actions.

Pushpadatta practised this deceit and it was not right. The fruit was bitter. Through the sin of deceit, she was reborn as a maidservant in the house of the merchant Sagardatt in Champapuri. Her name was Putimukhi — "foul-mouthed" — and from her mouth a constant stench emanated. Therefore, the wise should recognise deceit as the cause of sin and abandon it from afar. This deceit is the cause of the sufferings of animal births, the destroyer of lineage, beauty, fame, greatness, good destiny, wealth, and happiness, and the creeper that increases worldly existence.

Knowing this, those who have abandoned deceit and follow Jain dharma should, like experienced scholars, practise truthfulness and straightforwardness in thought, word, and deed. For only through sincerity can the soul progress on the path to liberation.

This story teaches that deceit — especially in spiritual life — is a grave sin. Pushpadatta, despite taking holy vows, maintained her pride and practised hypocrisy. The result was a foul-smelling birth as a servant. The wise should cultivate honesty and humility, for these are the ornaments of the soul.
